title: About
text:
Professional Background
Lina Andersson is a PhD student in the Department of Pediatrics at Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Sweden.
Her research is focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Using methods like flow cytometry, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-cell RNA sequencing, she investigates the cellular and molecular changes in disease development and progression.


Education
Bachelor’s degree in Molecular Biology from University of Gothenburg
Master’s degree in Molecular Biology from University of Gothenburg.


Personal Interests
In her spare time, Lina enjoys gaming, reading, and cooking.

title: How to Publish a Quarto Blog via GitHub
text:
When first making a Quarto blog, it can be a bit tricky to figure out how to publish it online. In this post, I will walk you through the steps to publish your Quarto blog via GitHub Pages.

Prerequisites

Make a Quarto blog project. You can do this by typing Quarto: New Project in the command palette.

This will create a new Quarto project with the necessary files and folder structure for a blog. You can customize your blog by editing the _quarto.yml file and adding your own content in the posts folder.

Next, start tracking your project with Git. Make sure you are in your project directory. You can do this by opening a terminal in your project directory and typing:

|# eval: false
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"

Create a new repository on GitHub and connect your local repository to it. You can do this by typing the following commands in your terminal:

|# eval: false
git remote add origin <your-github-repo-url>
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main


Publishing in GitHub Pages
You can now publish your blog using GitHub Pages, a website hosting service. This only needs to be done once

Make sure you are only rendering locally. You do this by freezing the blog to a static site by adding the following line to your _quarto.yml file:

execute: freeze: auto
If you have executable code in your project you’ll notice that a _freeze directory has been created. This directory stores the results of computations and should be checked in to version control. Whenever you change a .qmd file with executable code, it will automatically be re-run during your next render and the updated computations will be stored in _freeze.

Next, render your blog locally by typing the following command in your terminal:

|# eval: false
quarto render

Next, you need to configure the GitHub Pages deployment for subsequent invocations. You can do this by typing the following command in your terminal:

|# eval: false
quarto publish gh-pages

Add a “workflows” directory to your .github folder and create a new file called publish.yml in it. Add the following content unchanged into the publish.yml file:

on: workflow_dispatch: push: branches: main
name: Quarto Publish
jobs: build-deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: contents: write steps: - name: Check out repository uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - name: Set up Quarto
    uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

  - name: Render and Publish
    uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
    with:
      target: gh-pages
    env:
      GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
This file will contain the configuration for the GitHub Actions workflow that will automatically build and deploy your blog whenever you push changes to your repository.

Finally, push your changes to GitHub

title: How to add a GIF
text:
Here, I learned how to add a GIF to a Quarto blog post.


![](duck-dance.gif)

I also learned that you can add a GIF to a Quarto blog post by using the ![]() syntax in Markdown. The GIF file should be placed in the same directory as the Quarto file or in a subdirectory, and you can reference it using the relative path. Alternatively, if you leave the path empty, Quarto will look for the GIF in the same directory as the Quarto file automatically.
Isn’t that great? It makes me wanna duck dance!
